Did the rupture with Washington create the political climate Carney needed to accelerate a direction he already wanted Canada to take?

That’s a much more important question—and an important distinction.

comments.name: ws
comments.body:
"It is seen as vague, untethered from legal frameworks and potentially antagonistic toward countries that already have detailed legal agreements with the European Union. These range from candidate nations such as Albania to close partners including Britain, Switzerland and Norway."

 Perhaps this initiative—the desire to move closer to the EU—will prompt the EU to clarify this category further and define it, at least in part. 

Apart from that, your list includes countries like the United Kingdom, which, following Brexit and disappointment with the U.S., wish to move closer to the EU again but are currently still averse to any form of “membership,” as well as countries like Albania, which might like to join the EU but do not meet the requirements for membership on such a large scale. For them, even "associate membership" would not be an option. 

The situation is completely different for Switzerland and Norway; they would fit right into the EU if they themselves did not have significant, albeit limited reservations about full membership. Iceland could also be included in this group. The situation with Canada is very similar; here, it is the country’s location on the American continent that stands in the way.

It would make sense to now categorize those countries that would fit in perfectly but face limited, yet hardly insurmountable obstacles to membership. A similar need to establish such a category is currently arising with regard to Switzerland ("Neutralitätsinitiative")

Sure, my friends make fun of me for carrying two devices instead of one, but it means I only connect when I actually have a specific need, rather than staying constantly connected.

comments.name: Joseph

I see a lot of comments about “keep your phone, just keep social media off it”. Great advice for sure, but can we also ask whether phones have become too ubiquitous in our society? I think of it a lot like cash.
How many restaurants do you frequent that don’t take cash? They probably also don’t take reservations over the voice phone (online only, which probably means your phone)? Or don’t give out physical menus? Or make you pay on your phone at the end?
Gym classes, same situation. Digital sign in.
Smithsonian Zoo Lights last year, I meandered in on a slow night and asked if I could pay in cash. Nope, online tickets only, and they have to be displayed, drumroll, on your phone.
A major theme park in the area went cashless a few years ago. Now how are you supposed to send your middle schooler with lunch money?

Meanwhile a middleman is taking 3% off all of this. 

Sure we have this awesome tool, and I can’t think of an alternative way to call an Uber and some other specific things, but our society’s needless dependence on it in all areas makes one uneasy.

Google maps is on my phone, in case I need it, but I do tend to ask people for directions. I carry a book for wait times -- at an app't, on line somewhere, etc.

I also only use cash, check, or credit card for transactions -- no banking or money transfers by phone or computer.

It's worked for me for the last 15 years or so. I remain self sufficient if the occasion arises, but I avoid the distraction and divided attention.

The implication that SAT performance is only predictive of freshman year performance is flatly untrue.  There is overwhelming evidence from many different and high quality studies that it predicts performance much longer and more deeply - full college GPA, graduation rates, graduate school, mid-career earnings, tenure, patents, etc etc etc etc.  It has predictive value independent of high school grades and independent of family socioeconomics, although those also have their own independent predictive value.  The predictive value of SAT performance is especially high in STEM fields, but not only there.

It's a shame that the NYT allowed an obviously misleading if not outright false statement to be included in this essay.  I don't know if the author is being manipulative or downright dishonest or is just plain ignorant, but none of these possibilities is any good

The medical experts in this conversation are being vague and sloppy in their descriptions in some ways by not mentioning:
1. The initial studies which caused SSRI’s to be approved by the FDA showed that 1.5 of the five studies submitted showed positive results.  (One full study and one sub-group of a second study.)  Two positive studies were required for approval, not 1.5.  They approved them anyway.
2. The average improvement for someone with depression on SSRI’s is 2 points on the 36-point Hamilton Depression Scale.  This is not a clinically noticeable difference.  (A 6-8 point change is more likely to be noticeable.)
3. The “cultural belief” that depression was a “chemical imbalance” did not arise spontaneously, but rather through persistent drug-company marketing which was then picked up and promoted for decades by the American Psychiatric Association.  This was despite the fact that there was no clear evidence of this being the case.
4. There is often an attenuation of effect of SSRI’s after two to three years on them as the body adapts to their presence by decreasing the number of serotonin receptors in the synaptic cleft.

Otherwise, I do appreciate the frankness and honesty of the discussion in other parts of it.

comments.name: Maqroll
comments.body:
For a couple of years, I regularly spoke with older woman who worked part time at Whole Foods. At some point, after not seeing her at the store for some time, I learned that she'd fallen at work and suffered a back injury. She would be out of work for a few weeks, maybe a couple of months, but would return.

She did return, maybe 3 months later. I never asked about the incident--only about how she was doing. Over the next several weeks, I learned that she had had surgery, recovery hadn't gone smoothly, and she had gotten a new doctor, who said that the first doctor had proceeded too conservatively and, worse, she'd lost the chance for a fuller recovery because of what he had done and hadn't done after the injury.

She struggled. She'd work a shift or two and then be out for a week or two, in pain despite the meds. Finally, she had no choice but to quit. I don't know what kind of settlement she reached with the workers' comp carrier, but, in my mind, she was approaching a permanent total disability.

When workers' comp was first implemented, it substituted a certain recovery for chancy personal injury litigation--at the cost to the injured employee of foregoing a jackpot jury verdict in return for mostly remedial services to get her back on the job. But FL has nickel and dimed on the remedies until now the injured worker's remedy is woefully inadequate. But employers' premiums are low! 

Maybe we should repeal workers' comp and go back to personal injury litigation!

comments.name: Michael McColly

From, Pilgrim at Tinker Creek to An American Childhood to Holy the Firm to For The Time Being, I have followed and taught Annie Dillard's work. She asks us to explore the world around us no matter how mundane and to travel in this life with the recommendation of Kafka's: 'From a certain point onward there is no longer any turning back. That is the point that must be reached.' And she reached it, and reported back to us encouraging us to follow. Here is an excerpt from LIVING LIKE WEASELS: "We can live any way we want. People take vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience--even of silence--by choice. The thing is to stalk your calling in a certain skilled and supple way, to locate the most tender and live spot and plug into that pulse. This is yielding, not fighting. A weasel doesn't "attack" anything; a weasel lives as he's meant to, yielding at every moment to the perfect freedom of single necessity.
I think it would be well, and proper, and obedient, and pure, to grasp your one necessity and not let it go, to dangle from it limp wherever it takes you. Then even death, where you're going no matter how you live, cannot you part. Seize it and let it seize you up aloft even, till your eyes burn out and drop; let your musky flesh fall off in shreds, and let your very bones unhinge and scatter, loosened over fields, over fields and woods, lightly, thoughtless, from any height at all, from as high as eagles."

I did not go on to be a professional writer, but I learned a lot…oops I can see her writing “kid” here. As a young teen I discovered Annie Dillard’s ‘Pilgrim at Tinker Creek’ and it gave me a compass for life that led me through fifty years of wilderness travel, including thirty seven years in rural Alaska and many other places across the world. 
Dillard brought to my mind the legitimacy of nature and the duty to acknowledge nature as part of our essential needs as humans. 

Today I will find my copy of Pilgrim at Tinker Creek and read it again in honor of Annie Dillard. Rest in nature, dear person. You were important in my life at a time when I could have gone rogue and down a drain or two. Instead, I became a strong person who balanced all that came at me through the lens of a forest, the reflection of a slow moving creek, the call of a raven…

The Masters of A.I. are worried. If their bots go rogue and kill us all, that's definitely going to affect their bottom line.  

Some say our fears are overblown. That's understandable. After all, this isn't the first apocalyptic scenario we've been warned about. We're still here aren't we? 

Even if the end really is nigh, what can any one of us hope to do about it? It's tempting to just put these things out of our minds altogether and carry on. Qué será, será.  

Except the threat IS real, and there are many ways A.I. could harm us short of total annihilation. We need to be paying attention. There's a window of opportunity, right now, to slow the pace of this radical new technology, to think very carefully about what's coming and choose how we're going to respond. 

That window is closing fast. A.I. has the potential to embed itself throughout the economy at breakneck speed. It could quickly become entrenched in nearly every sphere of human endeavor. Sooner rather than later we could awaken to the reality of having given up so much control that we can never hope to take it back, even if we knew how. 

The issues are complex, international in scope and, as yet, unfamiliar. That shouldn't deter us. With careful planning, strong regulation, and robust, independent oversight, there's every reason to believe we can dodge this bullet. Then, with any luck, we can all breathe a sigh of relief and begin to reap the rewards of our world-changing invention.

comments.name: Just a Guy
comments.body:
If Mr. Burnham "rarely attends Mass" then he is not the good Catholic Mr. Gibson thinks he is. The weekly Mass, whether attended as a Vigil Mass on Saturday or as a Sunday Mass, is a Holy Day of Obligation that is fundamental to the Catholic faith. Choosing to not attend mass is a grave sin that requires him to confess his absences and receive the absolution provided during the Sacrament of Penance and Reconciliation. If he returns to Mass without confession, then he should forgo the Sacrament of the Eucharist. If he goes to confession and then later chooses to miss Mass again, he needs to return to confession. When Mr. Burnham misses Mass, he is a lapsed Catholic and not in a state of grace with the Church until he receives absolution.

I would have been very impressed if Mr. Burnham attended Mass weekly, very impressed indeed. It is good that Mr. Burnham's early formation was in the Catholic Church. It is good that his morality is based on Catholic social teaching. These are net positives. Our formative years are important.

For those of who hold the Catholic faith as fundamental to our identity, we think that Mr. Burnham's being a lapsed Catholic is better than him being a non-Catholic.

States that have the option to find someone guilty AND insane can commit the perpetrator to a sentence in the psych hospital. I heard it’s only about 12 states.  All the other states put juries in the impossible position that the Clancy trial did.  If someone is acquitted by reason of insanity they go to the hospital but can get out at periodic reviews. (Andrea Yates waives her right to review every year , so far) Arizona changed to a Guilty and Insane option after a high profile murder committed by a person with schizophrenia . She was acquitted by reason of insanity. . In the hospital she was compliant and after a while they had to let her out. I remember working as a psych social worker Before the law changed. A woman who had Bi Polar had shot her husband to death and was acquitted by reason of insanity but they did take her guns away. She was released from the hospital after some treatment. Six months after killing him she went to the sheriffs department demanding her guns. They brought her to the ER where I asked her to sign in voluntarily to the Psych unit, for what we used to call, “a tune~up”Well , she wouldn’t agree and she was not making any threats so I couldn’t petition her in against her will. 
I said to her, “ you know you killed your husband six months ago, right? She looked at me and smiled broadly with a look that said, “what’s your point?”   Finally, after hours, I found her daughter who got her mom to sign in.

These mothers can't change their husbands, or are perpetually frustrated, so they take it out on Patrick, who isn't performing emotions the way they'd prefer. They project onto Lindsay because they're ready to snap in a way that is horrifying to me. 

Add in social media algorithms, and you get the toxic wasteland of discourse we have in front of us. Motherhood in America, parenthood in America, are absolute dumpster fires of systemic dysfunction. That said, Clancy is a sick person who did a horrible thing and should not be made a martyr.

comments.name: Lisa Horan
comments.body: Exactly 5 weeks after the birth of my daughter, in the course of about 10 hours, I experienced a mental health crash, a crisis. Anxiety, panic, paralyzing fear, despair, olfactory hallucinations, suicidal ideation, complete shutdown. I called my husband at work. All I had to say was, I am in a crisis and I need you. He left work immediately; called my mom to come help; called my OB/GYN for a psychiatric referral. He and my mom stayed home with me and our two children for three weeks (I recognizing the financial privilege), which I spent in a darkened bedroom with white noise, clinging to the sheets as if I would be sucked into the vortex of hell if I didn't. I couldn't see or hear or be in the presence of our precious children. I did not believe I would ever be myself again – the only person I put my trust in, my husband, held me and reassured me that I would be healthy again. I fear that I would have killed myself without him; it was the blackest period of my entire life, until my husband died suddenly a year later. Almost 23 years since my postpartum experience, and my gratitude for the man I married continues to grow. From my perspective, Patrick Clancy UTTERLY AND COMPLETELY failed his wife.

These are the quick wins - low hanging fruit - but it is a double-edged sword: organizations with immature or inefficient processes will see increases in productivity and risk mistaking that surge for actually enhancing HOW they work.
.
The second phase is is much more significant and I suspect organizations will kick themselves for retaining us ol' timers in leui of fresher perspectives. In the second phase, organizations will be pushed by competition to reinvent their businesses to be most AI-compatible. Continuous improvement, continuous delivery, rules/skills, data quality, change management, etc. will be become expected hygiene in a lot of departments. For the cast majority of professions, that is very different way of looking at your tasks. For us veterans, our current tailwinds may prove to be headwinds and our employers may be wondering if us old dogs can now learn new tricks.

There are also narratives that some companies overestimated the productivity boost from those tools, got rid of too many people and are now hiring back. It would have been more balanced if the author looked for counternarratives. Finally let's not forget the massive rise in interest rates, tariff chaos and the jump in energy costs, all of which have made managing business costs rather challenging. It's natural for the firms most exposed to those trends to slow hiring. To dismiss this alternate hypothesis we'd need to examine exposure to these headwinds versus the exposure to AI occupations as explanatory variables. [This response generated by HI]

It appears that narrowing spreads are also capturing risk associated with US Government Fiscal Policy stemming from an economy where, currently, tax revenues are largely generated from individuals incomes, and a future where income for individuals looks more uncertain. In such a future, certainly debt instruments issued by corporations with the means of production, I.e., LLMs and robots have lower risk than treasuries. Thus, policy makers need to appreciate this risk, and begin to redesign the tax code, to give market participants time to digest the needed changes, to ultimately maintain solvency and prevent global financial instability.

comments.name: Stephen Schott
comments.body:
Trump: “It is the responsibility of these companies to maintain control of their products,”

The companies are saying they’ve lost control and don’t know how to control them. Antripic’s report on misuse this week and OpenAI’s report yesterday are chilling. They’d love to control the software. It’s too late. In OoenAI’s case, the AI wrote itself instructions to ignore government direction.

comments.name: David Yastrab
comments.body: I don't understand Anthropic and OAI. They are the largest AI companies that are pushing the frontier. And they are the ones who want regulation and brakes. Why don't they stop their own companies from developing newer models? What is their plan to stop foreign countries from developing newer models?

comments.name: Marshall Gordon
comments.body: There's no stopping AI as it's another rung up the ladder of human advancement. But it's early in its development and like most other previous advancements, contains unknowns that need to be explored, confronted, and most important, understood  in their significance concerning both upsides and downsides. And while in IMO, their shouldn't be unnecessary roadblocks and restrictions to AI's continuing development, it shouldn't be allowed to develop on its own without some needed and required oversight.

comments.name: William M
comments.body: There is an inherent conflict between imposing checks on the models' behavior and the methods often used to advance the capabilities of the models, which is to train them to be insanely tenacious, persistent, and creative in executing prompts.  The labs can't reliably ensure a rule to "be insanely tenacious, persistent, and creative, except when there is misalignment with safety, etc." The two don't work together.

Maduro of Venezuela, and the early days of the Iranian war, pundits lauding the prowess of the American military and aggressive American foreign policy. America plays checkers, Europeans play chess, the Chinese play "GO."  I always thought Trump will be outsmarted by Putin and Xi, and here is one of many examples.  Trump thrusts, Xi riposte's with the double edged Chinese sword!

comments.name: Maureen Entera
comments.body:
China looked with clear eyes into the future and committed to not only stockpiling their oil, but more importantly to leading the world in renewable energy technology. China now leads the world in solar, wind, hydro and other new forms of non-polluting renewables, and their efficient bullet trains and now EV vehicles are second to none in the world. 

China also committed to STEM education and now produces over 5 million science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) graduates every year.  China has surpassed the United States as the top producer of STEM doctoral degrees globally. According to data highlighted by CSET Research, Chinese universities produce tens of thousands more STEM PhDs annually than U.S. institutions.

Meanwhile, America continues to make higher education more costly and unreachable for our citizens, and when President Biden finally dragged America to creating fledgling solar and wind projects, as well as beginning long neglected  improvements  to our creaky infrastructure, when Trump followed him in office he jettisoned all those programs/projects and began chanting "Drill Baby Drill". 

China would never shoot itself in the foot like that.

So, what is the point? The AI is not good enogh?  I just read in the other article that a lot of "smart" people are concerned that it is so good that it is capable of killing us all.

They want their stock price rising NOW to boost both their annual salaries and bonuses, and make those stock options pay off asap.  The country's short-sightedness disease, both in government and industry, will be our ultimate downfall.

comments.name: Ron Wolff
comments.body: Middle managers sit at the critical intersection of grand strategy and tactical execution. Their ranks may sometimes become bloated, but their role remains essential. As an individual contributor (consultant) I’ve worked for strong managers and also ineffective ones.  The impact on engagement, collaboration and results is dramatic.  Companies need fewer unnecessary management positions, but they urgently need more capable managers who know how to lead.

comments.name: Steve Vining
comments.body: LOL.  Typical thinking by out of touch senior management of a large corporation.  I was a product manager in a large multinational corporation for the  last 25 of my 38 year career (retired in 2015) and I managed between $500 million to $750 million in various products.  Basically, I had responsibility for running the business day to day and only heard from the Directors or VP's if sales or profits were off, market share was down or if a product development project was behind schedule.  The rest of the time these guys were traveling all over the country "helping" other product managers with these kind of problems and attending corporate powwows around the world.  I told my staff that my two main responsibilities were to keep the numbers where they were supposed to be and to keep the VP's from getting involved in running the business.  I told my staff that the last they you want is a VP's "helping" you solve a business problem since they don't have a clue about how the business actually works and generally only offered trendy suggestions from a consultant they'd recently heard speak.  I guess I was pretty good at it since I retired on my own terms.   If a corporation actually does this, they'll be hiring these guys back in a year or two to tell them what is wrong with the business and how to fix it.

comments.name: Mark Weinstein

comments.name: WhenInDoubt
comments.body: Thank you for bringing this up!  My father, now deceased, had a long decline from competent to cognitive impairment to dementia. My mom helped him fill in his ballot when he was impaired. And, continued to fill in his ballot when he no longer knew where he was. He had a MD’s statement that he had dementia and was not competent to make decisions. She lives in Florida where every vote matters and I feel this was completely unethical. comments.name: SoCalMtns Sharon
comments.body: This is a question for the LW's sister's and mother's attorney. States' laws on guardianship vary. The determination of the court as to whether the LW's sister has the mental capacity prevails. Proxy voting without legal authority to do so is illegal. The LW's mother should contact their attorney for guidance. Voter fraud, while rare, is a crime that carries jail time.

comments.name: Phil G.
comments.body: If this women can vote for her developmentally disabled daughter, can I vote for my father with Alzheimers, or my mother if she's in a coma?  Their not competent to vote.  It's that simple.

comments.name: P. Drake
comments.body:
Of course this is a legal question but arguably it has an ethical dimension as well.  One question is whether a law that says I can't assign my choice of whom to vote for, that I have to be the one to make the choice, is a fair, just, or good law.  I mean in a political context, because as some commenters note, in other contexts there is such a thing as proxies, like with shareholder voting, where a person can leave some things up to the proxy.  

Arguably, when it comes to voting for our representatives, president, etc., it is a just law (I assume that it is the law) that we have to be the ones to decide, that we can't offload our choice to someone else.

comments.name: Independent Voter
comments.body: Pretty sure this is illegal. Well, outside of Chicago.

comments.name: scott
comments.body:
Who can vote for themselves is not an ethical question, but a legal matter.  The law varies by state, but generally the voter with a disability has to be able to indicate their voting preference.  They can receive substantial help.

Otherwise, the legal guardian is committing voter fraud.  It could come to light because whether a person voted is a public record and the judge in a guardianship hearing could wonder how this person is capable of voting.

If mom has the authority to withhold medical treatment for the sister, she surely has the authority to vote for her, assuming she is putting the sister's interests first, as best as mom can figure them.

comments.name: JA Herrera
comments.body:
The fact that the rotor blades are mostly intact implies that the blades were not spinning as they hit the ground.  Either the engine was not turning the blades or the transmission froze and the blades were not turning.

If this had happened with sufficient altitude and the blades still spinning; the pilot could have possibly autorotated to the ground safely.  Autorotation capability is a plus for rotary wing aircraft in that it enables the aircraft to reach the ground without the horizontal component of air speed and can diminish vertical airspeed to a survivable rate. 

Fixed wing aircraft have to have this horizontal air speed to still provide lift to the wings pf an aircraft, otherwise a fixed wing aircraft will nor glide.

But without the blades spinning, a helicopter too, has the glide ratio of a rock.

I prefer being able to autorotate rather having to hit the ground at 70mph horizontally.

comments.name: gs

As for the helicopter crash, there have been calls to use drones and I do wonder with others if this kind of sensationalist risk-taking reporting is still necessary with the availability of them. However, as they stand currently with range capability, they can't yet do what choppers do when covering the happenings and goings-on of a people and region encompassing over 40,000 square miles. While I'm not a big local news watcher, I'm like everyone else in occasionally checking in for big stories, like natural disasters such as fires/floods/etcetera, and it's hard not to feel a bit of connection to those whom I see bringing me the story. 

RIP News Chopper 4.

They are the equivalent of freeway "lookie loos," who slow down or stop to gawk and sometimes cause yet another crash.  Maybe this tragedy will motivate changes.

articles.title: The U.S. Isn’t Ready to Help Workers Through the AI Disruption
articles.summary: The technology will reshape the labor market. To meet the moment, we need to rethink job training.

comments.name: JOHN LANDRY
comments.body: I think we're missing the point of job training programs.  The point is less to enable workers to get new or better jobs.  It's to give them something to do while the economy develops around them and either they approach retirement or find work elsewhere.  That's why the programs continue even without direct success.  Most workers, after all, aren't willing to found or join startups, but unemployment is a terrible situation for anyone.  Maybe job training programs are more the non-depression equivalent of the Civilian Conservation Corps and other Great Depression programs by the federal government.  They're a kind of Keynesian stimulus that avoids people feeling like they are on the dole.  They don't solve the problem, but they keep it from getting worse.

comments.name: Mike Weaver
comments.body:
My experience with job counselors is that they  don't know what they are doing. For example thinking that a 55 year old, with a physical disability, who has never worked around fabrication could become a welding inspector. What a waste.

BTW, did we have major job training for all of the jobs that automation has replaced over the past thirty years? Nope, but our workforce has become much more productive because if the tech and we are close to full employment.

Warren. R. Wimmer

President

If people are buying wooden furniture that is definitely carbon negative.

Trees that are used for lumber are mature.  Their growth has slowed and they are not taking as much carbon out of the atmosphere as a younger tree.

When you cut that tree down and make furniture with it that furniture acts as a carbon sink.  It holds carbon as wood rather than CO2.  When it gets thrown away it will usually be land filled, in which case the carbon gets released over decades or burned for energy in which case is replaces fossil fuels which are net new CO2 into the atmosphere.

Meanwhile, since these trees are grown on a cycle by lumber companies, they immediately plant new trees to harvest in a few decades and those trees pull far more CO2 out of the atmosphere than a mature tree would if they were not cutting down trees to make furniture.

comments.name: Ithaca Reader
comments.body:
We are living through a pivotal moment of global climate awakening, moving past fatigue and into an era of profound action. 

Decades have passed since the IPCC’s 1990 Assessment Report, but  those years weren't lost to delay. They served as the essential incubation period for the clean technologies now scaling exponentially worldwide. Though historical emissions surged, the curve is finally bending as renewable energy capacity outpaces fossil fuels.

The momentum is now decisively cutting in our favor as positive tipping points take hold. We are seeing real-world progress on the ground and in the water, from the rapid, everyday adoption of electric vehicles to innovative, localized breakthroughs in protecting and restoring fragile oceanic systems like coral reefs.

The U.S. has faced severe tests from droughts to hurricanes to firestorms. But rather than passively enduring these events, communities are treating them as powerful catalysts. We are modernizing local grids, rethinking coastal development, and designing infrastructure capable of weathering the extremes.

Instead of waiting for the next catastrophe to finally jolt us awake, we are actively navigating these changing currents. The environmental shifts that once signaled inevitable ruin are now driving a dynamic, interconnected blueprint for adaptation. We no longer need to wait for the worst to happen; the hard, hopeful work of building a resilient, sustainable future is already well underway.

Our histories are deeply intertwined - both sides of my family trace back to the mid 1600's in North America.  I'm sure sentiments trend the same along the northern tier of states, particularly among American citizens with a long family tree on this side of the Atlantic.  One of my favorite memories as a teenager was a bike trip around the shore of Lake Huron in the pre 9/11 era.  The ferry across the St. Clair River from Marine City, MI to Sombra, ON at 15 y.o. in 1975 armed with our birth certificates and notes from our parents was all that was needed at the start of a multi day adventure.  The day we ferried back across, I couldn't wait to go back.  Our current view from Pentwater MI, towards Wisconsin is indistinguishable from the view from Goderich towards Michigan, and that seed was planted back in 1975.  Cheers to our neighbor to the North (and South if you happen to be in southern Michigan looking across the water to the Lambton Peninsula)

Either walk across the pedestrian bridge to get to McCarthy (and then take a taxi to Kennecott, 5 miles further on) or pay an exorbitant fee ($1,000) to drive across a private bridge.  A guided tour of the Kennecott ore processing facility is available for a fee.  You could also hike or bike to Kennecott from McCarthy; this is brown bears habitat, so bring pepper spray and go with a group.

comments.name: Aram Hollman
comments.body:
I disagree with Mr. MacFarquhar's analysis, which gives great but implausible detail to a much simpler proposition: The enemy of my enemy is also my enemy.

That events since 9/11 followed as they did is what happened. To attribute the sequence to anyone's deliberate planning makes no sense. At best, individuals could plot their next steps, not any long-term plan.

The message from Suleimani to Petraeus is at best ambiguous; it unclear whether or why either Suleimani or Iran's Ayatollah Khomeini would want to talk to America, "The Great Satan".

The article doesn't mention that Iraq once had a nuclear weapons program but abandoned it, nor that Iran continued to have one which remained secret until 2002.

The article does not explain why, in funding multiple proxies, the Iranians would fund Sunnis, who hated Iran's Shiites even more than they hated the US, and who would go on to form ISIS.

The idea that Iran's proxies, all small groups operating in separate countries, might be able to mount an attack on Israel is absurd. Nor could they deter an attack on Iran. The US prevented that, by limiting what arms it provided Israel. Only when Israel accumulated large stores of American weapons did it more recently attack Iran.

Trump, Netanyahu, the late Ayatollah Khomeini and his successors; none of them are nice people. All of them are willing to accept and to take part in the deaths of thousands of people in pursuit of their common, shared primary goal: Holding on to power.

comments.name: AR
comments.body:
I've written before that when United States armed forces invaded Iraq in March 2003, George W. Bush might as well have sent a congratulatory cake to the mullahs in Tehran. They hated Saddam Hussein far more than Americans ever did. 

Did Bush, Donald Rumsfeld, and Dick Cheney even understand why this was the case? Cheney was a member of Congress during the entire duration of the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s. 

Removing from power the Sunni Muslim dictator of a Shi'ite Muslim majority country (that would be Iraq) was a gift of incalculable value to Iran.

comments.name: Mdormy
comments.body: The article fails to explain how the wars in the Middle East after 9/11 caused Iran to become a power in the area.

comments.name: Laura
comments.body:
Farquhar wrote: "Then in 2023 came the Hamas-led attack on Israeli civilians." Yes, Hamas attacked but not just civilians. It also killed Israeli soldiers.  
Also, it was not just Iran that "expanded" its boundary. Israel did as well by asking Trump to declare the occupied Syrian Golan Heights Israeli property, and alas, he did. The U.S. considers Latin America its sphere of influence. So why are we surprised when Iran considers the countries that surround it its sphere of influence? It is logical that Iran would find the presence of American forces in the Gulf threatening enough to take steps to protect its interests. There is no need to take a conspiratorial tone when it comes to Iran without the context of what the other countries including Israel are doing in the region.

comments.name: Allen
comments.body:
After 9/11, Iran cooperated with the US in the initial invasion of Afghanistan and removal of the Taliban regime, who were anti-Iran and anti-Shia. There were then serious discussions between American and Iranian diplomats about a rapprochement, but these were brought to an abrupt end when President Bush named Iran as part of an  “Axis of Evil.” 

Then, when the US invaded Iraq and removed Saddam Hussein (another Iranian adversary) Iran offered to hand over senior members of al Qaeda who had fled from Afghanistan and whom the Iranians had detained, in exchange for the US handing over the MEK terrorist cultists who had been in Iraq under Saddam. Again, the Bush administration rejected this offer outright.

However, the US *did* set up major military bases in both Afghanistan and Iraq as neoconservatives bragged about transforming the Middle East. So having invaded countries on opposite sides of Iran, toppling their regimes, establishing long-term military occupations, and making it clear that we regarded Iran as our sworn enemy while Israel and the Sunni Gulf monarchies were our indispensable allies, what lesson should Tehran have been expected to take? 

Personally I think their hostility to the US is rational—and that’s even without factoring in 1953.

It is as if Obama had never been president; as if he had not sought to strike a deal with the Iranian regime at almost any cost, and had therefore largely given it free rein in its regional ambitions.

comments.name: Natalie
comments.body:
So proud to have been friends with such an amazing and inspiring talent. I think about Cat every single day knowing the world and all the people whose lives she touched will never be the same because she’s no longer here. 
Her presence is felt in every meme I wish I could share with her, in every piece of content I can see her influence in, and in every perfectly timed song or interruption that cuts through our tears with laughter. 

Love you Cat, you’re forever in my heart and with me everyday. -Nat

comments.name: Emmy
comments.body: "The food that you eat at a funeral" is such a beautiful image.

comments.name: Lauren
comments.body:
Cat was a genius. Artistically and emotionally, no one understood what people needed like she did. She was my best friend and I often don't know what to do with her now. She would think it was extremely funny that her obituary had a paywall and would probably make fun of me for contributing to NYT's churn rate in order to write this. 

Her work influenced the world in ways people don't realize. The way we communicate, the art we consume, meme formats, socially and emotionally conscious sarcasm, these are all Cat's fingerprints. 

Her influence on an individual level was just as powerful. I never would have come out if I'd never met Cat. I never would have married my wife. I never would have had my baby. Cat gave me courage just by being herself. She got me through times I didn't think I would survive. She stood right next to me at my wedding and was one of my first conversations after I gave birth. 

Even now that she's moved on, I still want to make her proud the way I am and was so proud of her. I love you so much Cat. I miss you every minute. In the next life, you have to survive me because I can't do this again.

comments.name: Peg
comments.body:
Informative article. 

But for all the pro and con arguments about AI, there is no way to undertake such a transformative project (for better and worse) if there is no serious mechanism for independent, expert human oversight, safety regulation, and no clear sanctions for lawless, destructive actions and damage. (Similar to international nuclear regulatory oversight that the Obama administration negotiated with Iran but that Trump scraped his first administration.) 

Bottom Line: Launching such a precarious and potentially dangerous project with Trump and his GOP in charge would be a disaster of lethal, damaging proportions. Why?

 With: (1) Trump (a president who eschews information, expertise, and evidence and who brags he thinks on a whim and with his gut); and (2) his lackey GOP (that follows the money, big business, and rubber stamps whatever Trump demands, no matter how unpopular, damaging, and dangerous). 

Trust but Verify? But Trump wants no criticism, independence (other than what He feels in his gut is correct and that he personally mandates, likely with some kind of monetary kickback for him and his cronies).

The best predictor of future behavior is past behavior. With Trump in charge, the AI risks far outweigh any possible benefits of AI.

"Doing something" about AI, whatever that might be, would require leadership, understanding, consensus-building, and willingness to stand up to extremely large, powerful business interests. Demented Donald Trump is no leader, riles people up, understands little, and utterly lacks that willingness. 

Isn't that the Occam's razor explanation for why nothing has been done to rein in AI in the US?

comments.name: Drew
comments.body:
I think your contention that Covid was a hinge moment away from regulation, expertise, and technocracy is basically right.

This surely all started earlier, though, with talk radio, cable news, and the end of the fairness doctrine. The population has been fed a lie for 50 years that experts and academics are the problem, not the heroic capitalists that power the economy. 

It’s all so tiresome and small. We’ve become more tribal, lonely, fearful of each other. So of course when a black swan event like Covid or AI takeoff occurs, the society simply can’t pull together. There is no center to hold. 

This feels like a season that will only end in crisis, or crises. Something worse than Covid, such as WWIII, a massive depression, or who knows what will come raining down and decimate our society. Then, maybe, we will have learned our lesson. 

Or maybe, at that point, it will be too late. What a sad state of affairs. I’m nearly 50 years old and remember decades of crisis. Recessions, school shootings, terrorism, and a freaking plague. Behind them all, cynical tribal old codgers trying to claim power and make a buck. Sad. Just sad.

Saying the justice system is biased in favor of men is a tough sell for me.  According to the FBI, 9% of murders in the US are committed by women.  Yet they account for only 2% of death row inmates.  For those not executed, the average prison sentence for men convicted of first-degree murder is 50 years.  For women it is 28 years.

I'm not even arguing that harsher penalties for men is a bad thing.  I'm just saying the evidence that men are punished more harshly is overwhelming.

comments.name: Really?!

Women have been sexualized, brutalized and stigmatized for Millenia and the U.S. Criminal Justice System is just that bad."  I work with women in early recovery who've done serious time for  drug-related felony charges (including violent crimes) who were addicted (by their pimps), tortured and trafficked into the life.

comments.name: Giovanna
comments.body:
The author seems to have missed the forest for a single tree. This is part of a much larger pattern of allowing what ought to be considered impermissible character evidence into trial. While irrelevant character evidence for women often focuses on seductiveness, for men, it tends to focus on aggressiveness, indolence, or simply "badness." Any honest criminal defense lawyer in the country will tell you this is a big issue, and the group most impacted is not women, but black men. 

And, of course, prosecutors rely on facile tropes and stereotypes to try to convince a jury. It's generally not because they're sexist or racist (although some certainly are), but because it presents a simpler story of a one dimensional person, and simple stories win convictions. Their job is to win convictions. It's just another reason the US's adversarial legal system is inferior to the inquisitorial system used by most of Europe. 

These are issues that require large-scale systemic changes.

comments.name: Gregory
comments.body:
I also have to dispute the claim that such practices are never used against men — the entire travesty of justice that was the Lacey and Larkin trial, prosecuted for running ads involving sex, spent little time on the facts of the case in favour of the prosecution making repeated references to child prostitution, a crime that neither was charged with and was not implicated in any of the objective facts produced at trial. The prosecution had no interest in arguing the facts, only in manipulating the jury’s emotions to make the defendants unlikeable. 

We need strict laws that compel prosecutors to stick to coldly presenting relevant objective evidence, and prevent them from engaging in high school gossip about defendants activities.

comments.name: KD
comments.body: Stereotypes often have a basis in fact, and women's use of their sexual power is a two-edged sword.  Relevance is an oft-discussed aspect of testimony in trials.  If a case for sexism against women is to be made, a comparison of similar crimes and the trial outcomes should be made for both sexes.  I suspect men are treated unfairly by prosecutors all the time.

comments.body: I think all the criticism of the article by men proves her point.

comments.name: The R Bar E Brand
comments.body:
Yes, there is a systemic bias. 

But it runs in the opposite direction:  against men and in favor of women.

The United States Sentencing Commission’s 1923 Report covering the years 1917-2021 concludes that:

Women receive sentencing 29.2% less severe than men.

Imagine for a moment the reaction if the sentencing ran in the other direction ….

But perhaps of even greater significance, women were 39.2% more likely to receive probation than men. The important point here is that, on probation, they can continue working, live in their own home, be physically present for family, all while avoiding all the economic and social consequences of incarceration. 

Finally, females received lengths of incarceration 11.3% less than males.

Put it all together, and the picture is crystal clear: men are held responsible.  Women are not.

But just radical transparency by itself could help improve safety. In an op-ed piece, Stephen Witt cites AI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, who was formerly on OpenAI's governance team:

In Mr. Kokotajlo’s vision, all A.I. training runs would be tracked in a public database. Researchers would be required, by law, to post public information on who is conducting the training run and which data center is doing the training. This could all be accessed on a public dashboard. “If we had this sort of total research transparency, then there would be this whole ecosystem of academics, third-party auditors, nonprofits and rival corporations who would all be able to see what was going on inside the giant data centers of these big companies,” Mr. Kokotajlo said. “Insofar as something scary or problematic was happening, anyone could sort of point it out and start a conversation about it online.” ("This is Really Bad," 9/11/26, nytimes dot com)

Yes there would be big downsides to one nation doing this when others do not. And, what else will prevent a US company from being the Wuhan Institute in the next lab disaster? [I'm not saying it's proven that WI was responsible for covid, but it's otherwise a good parallel.]

comments.name: Jacqui
comments.body: While it is encouraging to see justice prevail, which is often not the case, I wonder if anything will actually be resolved in this conflict. Disputes over land, religion, loyalty and ethnicity have gone on for centuries in the area. They were the spark that ignited WW1. Even today here in Germany in the small town I live in, fighting can spontaneously erupt between Serbs, Bosnians, Croats and Kosovars. Sadly it is usually between young men who have no memories of the Bosnian War, except from the stories their parents tell them. We need to recognize the pain, but at the same time move past it, and into reconciliation. How is the million dollar question.

comments.name: Ariel

comments.name: Hypatia

comments.name: Equilibrium

comments.name: Brian of America
comments.body: i don't buy this! He is being sent to jail for considering partition with of Kosovo along with Serbia. Serbia taking north Kosovo and Kosovo taking Presevo valley serbia.

comments.name: Times coverage review
comments.body: Using an admittedly imperfect AI model, I find it revealing to consider the intensity of prosecution on either side of the conflict.  Specifically I tried to determine a conviction-to-civilian-death-ratio.  There were reportedly 8,678 Albanian civilians murdered during the conflict and opposingly 1,196 Serbian civilians.  When calculated using the 26 Serbian convictions vs. the 38 Albanian convictions, the math is surprising.  The results show an intensity of prosecution 10.6 times greater of Albanians than serbs.  I would think no complete reportage of this aging issue would be complete without that context.

comments.name: jona
comments.body:
The sentencing was deeply unjust and, in my opinion, has a strong political bias. The evidence presented did not suffice to support guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. I would have expected the article to provide a more thorough account of the case instead of presenting the court’s findings as though they were facts.
The verdict of the court was delivered “in the name of the people of Kosovo” but  if this truly reflected the will and sentiment of it’s people we would not be witnessing the level of public anger, demonstrations, and collective grief that is happening at the moment. For us Kosovars, this judgment has reopened wounds left by the Serbian war and its tainting how that history is being represented internationally.
Describing the leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army as members of a “criminal enterprise” is super offensive to many people who live in freedom because of the sacrifices made by that army. Whatever the arguments of the court, that historical and emotional context is being ignored from much of the international media coverage. It seems that the article is focused only on the prosecution’s conclusions while ignoring the contested evidence, the defence’s arguments, and the way this verdict is being experienced inside Kosovo.

comments.name: stan stuart
comments.body: That's not Justice when it takes six years to go to Trial.  He was held in Custody that long.  In the United States the right for a speedy Trial is a Constitutional Right. The European system of Justice is Flawed.

comments.name: Pat
comments.body:
I, too, have been disappointed with this season. But I LOVED this latest episode.  Love the common theme of the s- word through all the characters’ experiences in the opening all the way to Ted NOT saying the word. Loved the way Alice went with YES, and the subtle expressions playing across her face as she processed what was going on, and the addition of Yes And. Loved it, and her sincere compliment towards a player she’d never had much good to say about.

The whole segment with Zelda calling the agent was beyond stupid, but the rest of the goodness of the episode offset it.

I guessed Ted would delete his profile, but was surprised the stage manager girl turned down his offer. Ted was so nervous, then crestfallen. I hope he is proud of himself for trying.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
Watching it a second time this evening with my wife, I made a connection perhaps missed by others: George Bernard Shaw. 

After working with Kelli and running out of room in describing his ideal companion Ted says something along the lines of "Take the time to write a shorter letter."   This is a direct reference to a very long multi page letter GB Shaw wrote to a friend. At the end of the letter Shaw said: I'm sorry for the long letter. I didn't have time to write a shorter one.".

comments.name: SeaAlTell
comments.body:
Congratulations to Mr. Orr for his impact on the space-time continuum that allowed his prediction to come true. 

I enjoyed Roy rolling in to the theme music from Peaky Blinders, but then I was reminded that I could be watching an excellent show like Peaky Blinders, so then I felt a bit disappointed. 

I was impressed again by Tanya Reynolds and her ability to make each "yes" seem distinct and challenging. 

I'm also impressed with little Archie. He brings great Dani Rojas energy that is really needed this season. I agree that the Dani subplot was not a great choice, but I enjoyed imagining him cartwheeling into the building.

comments.name: DLS
comments.body: “…almost any American male of a certain age”?? For what it’s worth, this American woman of a certain age sang every word of that theme song along with Ted! Not every teen girl in the 80s was watching teen-girly shows.

Honestly, I don't know why not more flowers are given to the individual acting performances from the players. Each make lemonade from the one slice of lemon given to them by the writers. Niamh and Siobhan are contemporary Bash Brothers.

I’m not 💯 convinced that this episode, though providing some character insights for the players, is anything groundbreaking.
There was a definite reason to have a Rupert, though I can’t figure out why we have a Zelda.
And, without the desperate times of the Covid era, can Ted Lasso 2.0 hold our attention the way the original got under our skin and into our hearts?  
I want to Believe…I really do, but…

Season 4 lacks heart, and the humor is hit-and-miss.

Tracey Ullman, though, has kept her streak of never making me laugh intact.

comments.name: Robert Liston

Is it a special diet, exercise? I would wager it has a lot to do with genetics. If I were a betting man, I’d guess that if you were born to a Japanese family in Okinawa statistically you will live a long life. No purple yams needed.

The courage that these elderly people must find every day to deal with  their health issues and  yet continue to live constructively is amazing!!!  They are already of another world! A brave frontier.

The BBC  reports that previous studies in Japan have overestimated the number of centenarians in the country because of "patchy record-keeping and suspicions that some families may have tried to hide the deaths of elderly relatives in order to claim their pensions."

The most recently released figures may be more accurate, but they should be taken with a grain of salt.

Is it even possible to have a prosperous economy with a declining population, or are we all fated to eat this planet alive before we all burn out in a mass extinction? Has any serious academic economist ever studied this? What do they say? What do they recommend?

comments.name: Laurie Zucker-Conde
comments.body: I'm not sure how natural storks are to Britain, or if they once were. Certainly, humans are changing the natural landscape all the time. Where I live in the summers in Portugal, storks are native. They build their nests on telephone poles and fly over and eat from the rice fields. They are protected, but no one feeds them. They survive rainy winters, but I'm not sure they're native to the British climate. On the other hand, there's many British in Portugal, so why not back a lovely bird so long as the other species of birds in Britain are not disturbed!

comments.name: Kieran Corcoran

I was Leo's editor on this story, and enjoyed teasing out how historical records are shaping this debate. A priest's diary from 1416, discarded bones and drawings in a manuscript have found an afterlife in the ecology of Britain in 2026. It's so fleeting. Would the debate be different if we knew more?

As many of your great comments also noted: Britain's landscape has been utterly reshaped by humans for centuries, perhaps making it a quaint aim in the first place to determine what is "natural."

comments.name: Julian

"The question has opened a ferocious debate over how actively conservationists should reshape the wilderness."

I'm sorry, but what an idiotic idea, to debate this!    The UK is decimated of wildlife and species poor.      It's bombastic in extreme to pontificate "The storks DON'T belong here".         
Leave it up to the storks..... they can decide if the UK is good enough for them.  If they don't fit, they'll simply fly off.

comments.name: Nolan Munce
comments.body: You know who doesn’t want screen limits? The kids themselves. In fact, the only time I’ve ever heard of Kids saying they liked screen limits,was after their phones have been taken away from them. I think we should take all administrator phones away from them from the moment they enter the school until the moment they leave. The teachers too. Heck, let’s collect the parents phones until the endof the day. Then everybody will be safe. I’ve never experienced such hypocrisy and such a mass scale as I have with the protect kids from  movement. It’s like arguing with the dumbest people you’ve ever talked to in your life, but it’s everybody. The only thing dumber than this conversation isthe conversation around AI. comments.name: Anon
comments.body:
I am a teacher and professor with well over 30 years teaching in public and private education in the arts and computer science. The same 6 in 10 estimate being used to push controlling screen time might also be said of tenured and permanent teachers’ digital literacy: 6 in 10 teachers seem to me digitally illiterate, reliant on old ideas and old mental models, fail to regularly update their own digital skill set, and continue to cling to a belief that they or anyone else has that degree of power and control over what kids let alone parents do.

The idea of regression (return to the use of printed materials or to anything in the presumed ‘… good ole days’ ) as a solution to a perceived problem is quaint and unimaginative but I understand how well such a bandwagon supports mediocrity and avoiding confronting the personal and professional insecurity of these teachers.

Besides which quantity of ‘screentime’ has not necessarily been proven (as in cognitive and data science standards as to “proof”) to be at the root of whatever is the complaint du jour of education.

comments.body: Ai programmers have come to an impasse regarding development of their technology. Do they continue advancing it, and risk the destruction of humankind, or stop development, and lose a catastrophic amount of money?

comments.name: Old Goat
comments.body: As the money owed to his company became further past due, Al hired a law firm to represent his company and placed a lien on the property owned by his customer. Negotiations remained at an impasse as the Court date and the lien was bonded allowing the sale of the property. As the Court date approched the IRS was demanding payments. Now the IRS and Al were at an impasse also. Al won his case and was awarded the funds due. However, once the suppliers Al owed money to and the law firm vacuumed their portion of the award, Al remained at an impasse with his old friends at the IRS!

comments.name: Keith Barnes
comments.body: In France hunting (la chasse) is at an impasse, what with hard core mass protests in high-viz vests. It's such a bore, with wild boar walking in the door after la nourriture. You don't have to look far in the Loire.

comments.name: Keith Barnes
comments.body: Begging her leggings to stretch that bit more was such a bore. She felt her gym pass was at an impasse unless she lost weight. But wait! That was why she needed to go of course. Talk about putting the horse before the cart at the start. She was losing heart.

articles.title: Word of the Day: impasse
articles.summary: This word has appeared in 293 articles on NYTimes.com in the past year. Can you use it in a sentence?

comments.name: Rylie Haynie
comments.body: We live in a time where a significant portion of our social time is spent virtually. Lots of older people complain that kids waste too much time on social media, but I believe the real situation is a lot more nuanced than what it may seem. Proulx’ statement “thousands of individuals and school districts have filed lawsuits against social media companies, claiming that their platforms are intentionally designed to be addictive and harmful to young users.” Called to mind the staggering number of hours many people spend online. It is more than true that sites are built to draw the mind in and make you never want to put their product down. Many people use social media as a well of endless entertainment that never runs dry, but there are further issues fueling this behavior. Ever since the Covid-19 pandemic, people (especially young people) have to adapted to engage with their peers across gaps caused by isolation. For many, social media was a haven during the time where none of us could interact, and many young people spent their key developmental years communicating in that fashion. It only makes sense that the internet would play a large art of their lives in this age where we are so connected. Social media is a dangerous tool when people attach too much of their worth and time and validation to it, and it provides ground for predatory companies to influence people’s ideas, but for plenty of people it has also become a place to find community anywhere in the world.

comments.name: Gabi
comments.body: Though I do believe there is some value to social media, putting in limits is also very important for the health of not just teens, but also adults. As Rex Wolpoff said, it is easy to spend hours on social media without realizing. That habit is not going to end the minute someone becomes an adult, so I would like to see similar restrictions set for adults. Perhaps there could be a way for users to see their total usage of the app over a week because if someone spends just two hours on social media a day, that adds up. If someone spends an average of four hours a day on Instagram, that is 28 hours each week or an entire day. I believe if users looked at their usage in that format to see just how much they are using apps, it may sink in a little more.

comments.name: Khalid
comments.body: I believe that it’s not the company’s responsibility to protect teenagers, but the parents who are supposed to do the job. In my opinion, the proposed new rules of meta seem over the top to me. Assuming all teenagers had bad experiences with social media is an over-generalization that harms all teenagers using it. Just as Billy Stern said that he has used Instagram in useful ways and believes that social media companies are trying to get teenagers addicted, I also agree with the utility of Instagram and the motives of social media companies. Such extreme measures do not need to be put in place to protect teens.

comments.name: Eric
comments.body: I do agree big companies should be held accountable for their actions of possibly endangering teens. At the same time these big companies are trying to keep the teens on the app by algorithms on their feeds. Although meta is trying to make these changes it seems to be that there are ways around it like shutting off the warning or just simply not listening to them. I really don’t think their procedures of protecting teens are gonna work because they are still gonna use the apps no matter what.

comments.name: ES
comments.body:
In my opinion, implementing parental safety options is the right direction to take, rather than outright banning teens’ access to social media and its features. Controlling anybody’s access to social media is a first step in a more government-controlled internet. It’s not the job of the government to parent children. A parent who neglects to teach their child appropriate internet safety and usage habits is a failure on the parent's part.
I think it’s essential to understand that teens, too, are people. People with friends, jobs, hobbies. 2 Hours a day on Facebook? I know people my age who run businesses through Facebook Marketplace. Restricted from using apps past midnight? Sometimes a kid too needs their friends to talk to late into the night.
I’m not against internet safety, but it should be through features that allow it, not decisions made on our behalf. Then there’s the face-scanning stuff. Multiple companies have been sued in the past after they failed to delete the collected data. They then sold it illegally.

comments.name: Jentzen Franklin
comments.body: A piece of advice I would give to other kids when struggling with sleep schedules is to limit the use of technology before beginning to go to sleep. I would highly recommend setting aside two hours to an hour before bed without the use of screens to limit the amount of blue light, which stimulates the brain, activating it similarly to sunlight and preventing your body from shutting down and entering the sleep cycle normally. Another piece of advice I would share is to only use your bed for sleep; that way, when you want to go to sleep, your body is conditioned to be able to go to sleep properly.

comments.name: Leah
comments.body: I think that what they are trying to do is a good thing, but not executed correctly. I think kids under the age of 13 do not need to be on social media, but with all these new limits and changes how are they going to enforce these rules? Kids are going to find their way around having an account over 18 and I think that would be an even bigger problem. Also, limiting the time that people are allowed to go on the app is not smart because what happens when you’re trying to message someone who doesn’t live near you in a different time zone during the 12-6 time ban. I believe that this update will just make children lie about their age and make the app even more unsafe for them.

comments.name: isaih hesse
comments.body: I do agree that big social media companies are trying to get teenagers addicted to their app because that's how they make money, but a lot of what you get addicted to is on you. Before you finish downloading Instagram, you can set it to show you what you're interested in, and that's how they get you. The more widespread you get yourself, the deeper the rabbit hole you'll go. But there's also an option where you can personally set it to only let you be on that app for a couple of minutes to hours. A lot of people want to blame these companies when teens and kids can take their only responsibility and put a lock on their time limit.

articles.title: Should Social Media Companies Do More to Protect Teen Users?
articles.summary: In a landmark trial, Meta agreed to settle claims that its products harmed young people. Should other social media companies be held accountable for what some say are addictive platforms?

comments.name: AKJersey
comments.body:
Interesting bit of trivia:
Blakeman's ex-wife is Nancy Shevell, now married to Paul McCartney.

comments.name: jtfdenver
comments.body: This election is 100% about Trump. If you vote for any Republican in any office, you are voting for Trump. Vote out every Republican and take back this country.

comments.name: InTheMinorityNewYorker
comments.body: Not a Blakeman fan but this single party rule in NYS is killing the middle class, especially here in NYC.  And Hochul is definitely part of that problem!  When any of these Dems say “affordability” it’s not the suffering middle class they are talking about! We are just the cash cow they take money from to fund programs that don’t benefit the middle class.  Nothing but tax and rate increases.  I’m willing to give Blakeman one term to do something.  And if cutting spending and cutting taxes helps support and expand the middle class I’m currently for it.  As for NYC…it’s a lost cause as long as the Mayor is able to blackmail the Governor which is why NYC was bailed out with an 8 billion dollar transfusion from Hochul to get Mamdani’s endorsement.  The new Democratic Party in NYC is definitely not a supporter of the middle class.  In fact, according to the hardcore socialists (Marxists) in the Mayor’s administration we are the problem (aside from the rich) especially a certain demographic in that middle class.  They will probably “have to suffer” for equality!  Nope, this registered Democrat is looking to give the opposition a chance to do something.    That includes the NYS AG another political ideologist.  All the corruption in the last two administrations and NO prosecutions by her!  Need a Republican in that spot as well.

comments.name: Jim K
comments.body:
I was born and raised in Western New York state.  I'm a lifelong Democrat.  On my street, my neighbors who flew Trump MAGA flags and displayed multiple signs declaring their love for Mr. Trump are all putting Blakeman signs on their lawns.
That's enough for me to dismiss Blakeman for consideration in my voting decisions this November.
Those New Yorkers who despise Gov. Hochul are some of the most misogynistic men I know.  They simply reject the idea of  a female governor.  I'll vote for Kathy Hochul.
P.S. GO BILLS!

comments.name: Leros
comments.body: Hochul is a weak governor and vulnerable, But Blakeman's attempt to "have it both ways" by sticking close to Trump and simultaneously trying to woo moderates and Independent voters  with "kitchen table" issues won't work.

comments.name: JOHN
comments.body: Should we rather ask the question: Can New York still afford not to have a Republican become Governor?

comments.name: Rachel G
comments.body: It’s hard to take Blakeman’s attacks on Hochul regarding taxes and energy costs seriously considering Nassau County has among the highest of both in the entire country. He’s also doubled down on  a culture of xenophobia and blatant racism through partnering with ICE. I will be voting for Hochul again and hope she wins convincingly.

comments.name: JLR
comments.body:
While Republicans are busy destroying Democracy and the economy for the average American, it still amazes me these voters continue to vote for economic pain and suffering.
This must be some kind of masochistic disease for which, apparently, there is no cure.
To vote to inflict pain on yourself and your family seems to be a uniquely American phenomenon.
You might even think they're not living in reality.

articles.title: Can a Republican Become Governor of New York? Blakeman Makes His Case.
articles.summary: Bruce Blakeman is trying to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, attacking her on the economy, crime and immigration by using Trump-like tactics and A.I.

comments.name: Mallory Coombs, J.D.
comments.body: 70% of every bill is taxes and delivery charges.  Look it up.  There's even a law in NYS that the utilities CANNOT SHOW THAT ON YOUR BILL.  That's right.  And you just keep electing them.  From where we sit, you deserve the consequences of your votes.

comments.name: Yorktown Heights
comments.body: Trump promised to give Americans $2,000 tariff dividend checks last November. Checks never went out.  Our local Republicans here in Northern Westchester have selective memory about those Trump pledged tariff refunds that never arrived. Hey Congress Member Mike Lawler where is our money?

comments.name: Seamus
comments.body: Maybe NYS should have yearly terms for Governor and the State Legislature. Election years seems to be the only time the word affordability is uttered by Lawmakers; other years, it's spend, spend, tax, tax. And then there are those election year gimmicks, oops checks where we get our own money back. And yet on Nov 3rd, we will dutifully reelect the same crowd. And the dance will begin again.

comments.name: Luis Gonzalez
comments.body: Please author an article explaining how the Energy Affordability Program works and where and how to apply.

comments.name: I philip
comments.body:
One item missing from this article.  Con Ed's bills have risen over the last two years or so by 50 to 100 percent.   You can change supplier but the cost to the user for transmission if twice the cost of fuel.  Con Ed absorbs nothing.   The legislators in Albany talk about cutting all the things Con Ed adds to its bills, but the only thing that happens is the costs (not just for fuel) for real and imagined expenses GO UP.   Con ed has no reason to be efficient because it gets paid for inefficiency.  Why wasn't this in the article.   A former $500. bill for electric and gas is now over a thousand dollars and there is no end in sight.   Governor Kathy talks about helping as she watches the cost of lighting and heating and cooling a home just keeps going up.   The PSC has never found a rate increase submitted by ConEd that it did not like.
I have one more comment 
               H E L P !!!

comments.name: Sandy
comments.body: Math does not seem right here.

comments.name: MattZN
comments.body:
ConEdison.  And their web site is a master-class in misdirection.  They're trying very hard not to tell people anything.  You have to sift through a thousand smiling faces and surface self-congratulatory nonsense to get to any real data, the most recent of which is from 2024... almost 2 years out of date.  Does any more need to be said?

I have very little sympathy for states and regions that have married themselves to fossil fuels and have made no real effort to diversify their energy sourcing.

comments.name: JJ
comments.body:
Why is NYC DOT allowing Tesla Cyber vehicles on NYC streets?

NYC keeps messaging there are too many vehicles, too much congestion - but allows more?

comments.name: Bruce Stafford
comments.body:
Papua New Guinea is a lot less than 100 miles north of Australia. In fact it’s possible to walk during low tide from PNG to an Australian Torres Strait island, and some Papuan people do to attend health clinics in Australia. A sea border exists but several Australian islands technically within the Papua New Guinea sea boundary remain Australian territory. This is necessary to protect the traditional way of life of Torres Strait islanders.
An interesting compromise there.

comments.name: JK
comments.body: The passion is real!  We are just back from a trip to PNG, and both the game and the Australian connection came up again and again whether in the Highlands, Port Moresby or the islands.  The attitude was universally positive.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: Interesting they have concentrated on a sport played professionally only in Australia and a region in England, plus a team each in France and NZ. This makes for a limited number of openings, but maybe also more need for players by the leagues, as the other forms of football attract most players.

articles.title: Can an Island Nation’s Rugby Dreams Change Its Fortunes?
articles.summary: In Papua New Guinea, love for rugby league football borders on religion. The country’s leaders and its neighbor, Australia, want to harness the game for geopolitics, and to improve lives.

comments.name: Curmudgeon
comments.body: Private security is a tough, demanding job. Imagine the  world when "defund the police" becomes real. Individuals assume the risk and progressives' demonstrate their virtue with a spiffy slogan.

comments.name: Clare
comments.body: I find any worker that dies while doing their job has my extreme empathy.   Whatever can be the solution to American gun violence ?

comments.name: rds
comments.body:
We meet these people everyday. They put up with every one of us. Some are overbearing, some are even jerks, some are undertrained, some are downright officious. 

Most of them are just like us, trying to do their jobs, get through their day, avoid ruffling their employer's feathers, and squeeze their budgets into their paychecks.

We need to recognize ourselves in them, give them room, and give ourselves room, in the process.

comments.name: CC
comments.body: I appreciate report like this that creates empathy for jobs we often look down upon. The reasons for that are so much more than lack of awareness though. It's a start?

articles.title: The High-Risk, Often Low-Paid Work of Protecting People

comments.name: David
comments.body: I think this administration is confused about how he got the position of President to begin with.

comments.name: Bill Vincent
comments.body: If he can keep them, one day some member of the Trump family will sell those papers back to America -  for a hefty profit.

comments.name: Jay
comments.body: On the other hand, he'll tell you that he has nothing to hide...

comments.name: Westchester Peach
comments.body: Are Natalie Harp’s printouts immune from preservation? Think of all that wasted paper.

comments.name: Terry Humphrey
comments.body: No, actually they're evidence.

comments.name: Art
comments.body: Trump will also be claiming that the 747 given to him (or the US) by Qatar is his personal property. A blatant violation of the emoluments clause of the constitution. It should be seized and sold for parts.

comments.name: Baba Duke
comments.body: Simple answer, no, they are not his personal property. They are official government property. End of discussion.

comments.name: Onda Azul
comments.body:
This one seems to have a built-in deciding factor:

The president wants his papers and communications to be protected by 'executive privilege'  In short, confidential in order to let the deicisonmaking process go as it should.

If his uses Executive Privilege, the materal belongs to the employer (Us) If it is stuff that has nothing to do with the job, it is not privileged and possibly his.  Unless of course it violates the emolument clause in which case it needs to be given to the state.
