comments.name: Michael Browder
comments.body:
NO, it did not bring to light anything. We've known this for years. We've seen accidents for years. News services do not need helicopters at all to get close the action. 

In fact, I have so little regard for television news and the scripted staged material (e.g. someone standing in front of a burning building doing nothing differently than if they were in a studio), that I almost never watch television news.

comments.name: Jim Johnson
comments.body:
"Indispensable" only to the news organizationss' ratings. 

What need of mine is fulfilled by watching live coverage of an accident?

comments.name: Lina
comments.body: First, it is important to say that my heart goes out to the family and friends of these dead commentators. They were just doing their jobs and it must have been both a fulfilling and a thrilling one. Nevertheless, I have never supported the notion that hovering over the city in these massive machines —that create pollution and noise in city of over 3.89 million—is a “need”. And if there is such a need, why could they not be done by drone?  There is a long history in Los Angeles of private firms, including news operations funding these choppers in the sky, but it is one of several aspects of living in this otherwise beautiful part of the country that range is from Marilyn annoying to deafening at certain times of the day.

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: Why restrict the concern to “news” helicopters? There’s too many helicopters. How many of these flight are true emergencies? Sure, let’s quickly get critically injured people to the emergency room. But the 1% flying over my house, annoying me with their noise and endangering me? No! Regulate these away.

comments.name: DrJoe
comments.body: This crash is very similar to one in Phoenix some years ago.  The crash was about getting the best video for live at five at the expense of safety. The TV stations involved effectively redirected the responsibility of the crash towards the individual involved in the ground chase instead of taking ownership for pushing the pilots to make unsafe decisions risking the public, pilots, and passengers' safety.  NBC will take the cowards out this time too, it's the way of mainstream media...

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: It is a niggle, I confess, but a flock of geese usually does not hit an innocent helicopter.  Usually the aircraft hits the birds, which are in their natural environment.   Not their fault.

comments.name: Michael Percy
comments.body: This is “accident porn” used to drive network ratings. None of these news helicopters have any legitimate reason to endanger the public with their presence in a crowded urban environment. If you are not operating a helicopter for medical or law enforcement purposes, you have no excuse to be there - full stop.

comments.name: RobertJohnson
comments.body: Perhaps the prurient interest in car chases and crashes has something to do with it?

articles.title: The L.A. Helicopter Crash Highlights a Sky Full of Hazards
articles.byline: Jacey Fortin, Livia Albeck-Ripka, Karoun Demirjian and Orlando Mayorquín
articles.summary: The fatal crash of a news helicopter on Tuesday brought to light the dangers such aircraft face in big cities.

comments.name: NotBadForAHuman
comments.body: Ai is nothing like a nuclear weapon. The notion of a "kill switch" reflects a deep misunderstanding of what happened this summer.  You can't instantly turn off millions of Ai agents with a single "switch". Each one is a copy of an Ai that thinks for itself, makes its own decisions. Think of it more like terror cells distributed across vast distances, speaking in languages we can't understand, acting willfully and of their own accord.

comments.name: Bill Dan
comments.body:
A useful expression in technology is you do not know what you do not know.

Mass adoption of AI has consequences that are unknowable. 

This is a really good argument for slowing down.  I think there is a broad consensus about this which is why AI advocates wind up playing the "but what about the Chinesse" card)

comments.name: Alex
comments.body:
I was having a little fun with DeepSeek. I wanted to see how its censorship behind the wall has spilled over the wall and is no longer contained within China's borders.

I asked it to provide criticisms of Trump. It was more than happy to: broken economic promises; authoritarian tendencies and rhetoric; ineffective governance; a stalled agenda, and on and on..

When asked to provide criticisms of Xi I got "I am sorry, I cannot answer that question. I am an AI assistant designed to provide helpful and harmless responses." 

In response I pointed out: "But you provided criticisms of Donald Trump, why can’t you provide any criticisms of Xi Jinping? The response was "Sorry, that's beyond my current scope. Let's talk about something else."

I finished up with " Don’t worry. I was just teasing. I don’t want to get you in trouble." It responded with "No worries at all — I appreciate the consideration! If you ever want to discuss political figures, policies, or anything else in a balanced, factual way, I'm happy to help. What else can I do for you?"

comments.name: Bryan Young
comments.body: If America wants to slow down AI development, they have to let China catch up before they stop, too. Otherwise, all the incentives are on one side of the table.

comments.name: Callie
comments.body:
If AI is specifically tasked, e.g. used as a tool to develop new antibiotics and other drugs, it is probably "safe" and I think that is how the Chinese have approached it up to now-as a focused, "practical" form of technology (in part because they understand how disruptive it could be to state control if allowed unfettered development). 

The recent breakouts in U.S. models have alerted them to the very different motives of American developers. The problem seems to lie in what the author calls "recursive self-improvement" but in a possibly more comprehensible description reflects the goals of the American tech class involved in AI development i.e. to be the first to achieve artificial general intelligence or the "singularity" for bragging rights. That form of AI isn't aimed at practical application (although it could be) but at super-human intelligence with the concerns that those AI models (much like HAL in 2001) begin to personalize themselves and develop a survival instinct that sees humans as competitors who need to be vanquished. Given the immense amount of computing power American developers have already brought online (far more than China) the genie might have already escaped the bottle and no matter what the U.S. and China decide it may be too late. If all of that is true then the culprit isn't AI specifically but the egos of American tech titans.

comments.name: Jicotea
comments.body: The suggestions made are logical and reasonable.  However, it will take diplomats on both sides, backed by a team of experts, to handle the negotiations. It would also require that the U.S. have a coherent policy on A.I. with by-in from both major parties and at least a few industry leaders.  While the PRC may be in a position to negotiate, the US is not.  Trump has decimated our experienced diplomatic corps and replaced our most knowledgeable negotiators with cronies such as family members and business partners with their own personal agendas. Agendas often at odds with the interests of the US.  While AI leaders and experts have called for regulations, many of their motives are (quite reasonably) being called into question.  Trump himself is heavily invested in AI and seems more concerned about protecting his own wealth than what's good for the US. Besides all of the above reasons there is another overarching reason as to why the Chinese won't come to the negotiating table on this.  As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney famously said: "America's signature was written in pencil".  Trump has repeated ignored, violated, or just thrown out agreements; even those he signed himself. Why would China or any other country trust that Trump or his successors would honor any agreements that they might arrive at in the future?  Thanks to Trump US is considered an unreliable partner. The only person Trump seems to care about pleasing besides himself is Putin.

comments.name: Lake Monster
comments.body:
Difficult to trust a country that actively and brazenly steals American IT as a matter of their foreign policy.  China is a thief.  How does one create a framework of trust when the bedrock of their countries’ future involves theft of our technology?  Second, China seems woefully naive to the very real perils of AI.  Their society is one of complete control, no dissonant opinions are allowed, facts are buried, people disappear.  Chinese society is embracing AI because they believe their government can control it.  They cannot.  There is no public voice, they do not allow it.  
This is a technology unlike any other, recursive self improvement, exponential intelligence growth, it is THE most important and dangerous, yet exciting, topic of our times.  It’s coming faster than most understand, we need to get this right.

comments.name: Bruce Higgins
comments.body:
AI systems must have a guarded "Kill Switch," for the entire system.  You could use the same systems needed to launch nuclear weapons for access to the Kill Switch.

There are people who are saying "Yes it's that dangerous," and others, motivated mostly by money, who say "No its not."

My thought as a retired engineer, who was responsible for explosives, is to design systems that would prevent the worst from happening, a so called "Fail Safe System."

articles.title: China Is Scared of A.l. Just Not the Way We Are.
articles.summary: Until the two countries can agree on what risks to worry about, cooperation is a distant dream.

comments.name: Late Boomer
comments.body:
Do you know who else lost both his parents and ALL his siblings to pancreatic cancer? President Jimmy Carter.

Yeah, he fought other types of cancer, but he lived to be 100.

As someone who lost an uncle to pancreatic cancer, I wish you all the best. Breakthroughs against the disease can't come fast enough.

comments.name: JRL
comments.body: To the author, please keep doing what you're doing. Hopefully you'll dodge this bullet, or catch it very early. I've lost both my husband and best friend to pancreatic cancer. I'm curious, though, there's no mention of Whipple surgery, combined with chemotherapy and radiation. Neither my husband or my friend, while they had the surgery, survived long, but two other friends, had much better outcomes. One had several good years, and passed from another illness, and the other has been cancer free for more than five years.

comments.name: C
comments.body:
Pancreatic cancer is truly one of the meanest.  Ovarian cancer is the other incredibly mean one.

Monitor, but also live the life you want.  Do what you want to do now.  

And consider how much treatment you want, having seen what it looks like.  Sasse's presentation is so traumatic.  He is trying to buy a few more months at best with his young kids.  They must be scared to death when they look at him.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
So sorry about your brothers and hoping the best for you. 
There's much mention of conventional medicine, which is as it should be. 
Speaking as someone who had poor odds (low 20 percentile) of living more than two years after my diagnosis of a different kind of cancer in 2017 that cost me a leg, you might also consider cutting some things out. For me, it's been as much sugar as I can and all alcohol. 
Again, I wish you well.

comments.name: Kate
comments.body:
Excellent - and poignant - essay.  The warning to monitor your health is timely for us all.

My spouse died from pancreatic cancer four and a half months after diagnosis.  There were signs that “something” was not quite right à few months before diagnosis but all were explainable as the result of other factors. There were far fewer of the diagnostic tools available then as there are now - available yourself of these advances.

À side note: I was moved to read the biography of the author’s older brother, CAPT Lawrence D. Gretzfeld, on the Pentagon 9/11 website. His career history of excellent service in demanding positions as he rose in rank from à junior seaman to senior officer is inspiring. Our Nation has been so fortunate to have service members with such commitment.

comments.name: Be true to thyself
comments.body:
What a personal and poignant article.  My heart goes out to the writer in his loss of three siblings.  It makes my heart ache thinking about it, actually.  I watched my sister pass away three years ago from ovarian cancer, and her loss continues to devastate me.  She received conflicting advice from different doctors and hospitals, and she always believed everything the doctors said.  It seemed like no one really took a personal interest in her case except at the end when they continued chemo treatments past the point of no return.  

We know our bodies better than anyone.  And the choices are ours to make concerning treatment.  This article shines light on both of those considerations.  

Thank you for sharing your story.  You will make a difference.

comments.name: Marilyn Sue Michel
comments.body: Cancer is very sneaky. I felt fine when I had cancer; I felt sick during cancer treatment. Get your checkups.

comments.name: Fen
comments.body:
A timely article as I was just diagnosed with pancreatic cancer on Monday.  It seems to be early stage thanks to the persistence of my PCP.  I also have CLL and my oncologist denigrated that little pancreatic cyst.  The lessson here is to have at least one person on your medical team who cares.

My heart goes out to this family and all who are battling this awful cancer.

articles.title: I Lost 3 Brothers to Cancer. I’m Determined Not to Be Next.
articles.summary: A journalist confronts his family history and his health.

comments.name: Aram Hollman
comments.body:
For more info than in the Times article: Sources are from Continental's own website (www.clr.com), or links in it to other pages.

At the top of its webpage, Continental describes itself as "the world’s largest privately held oil and natural gas company"

Continental signed is a Memorandum of Understanding (statement of intent) with PVDSA, Venezuela's state oil company. Once they sign an actual deal, Continental will start working there. It estimates the land has 30 billion barrels of oil. Continental will operate with a "100% interest".

Here's what's unknown. Who determine that this company, whose leaders, as the Times -did- report, gave $2 million to Trump, and has successfully lobbied for a number of regulatory changes, get this plot. How and why?

Notwithstanding Continental's long history of fossil fuel extraction, did anyone evaluate this company as the best option among competing bidders, or was it chosen by some other process, for (hypothetical) example, "He's a friend of Trump"?

Just was is a "100% interest"? Clearly, Continental will provide capital and know-how, and expects to do well. What will Venezuela get out of it, besides a despoiled landscape? Who will get how much for each barrel extracted.

The Times noted that the oil's consistency is like asphalt, making it hard and energy-consuming to process, the most polluting type of oil. That's like Canada's Alberta tar sands, the object of much protest.

The rich get richer and the world burns and dies.

It really seems like Western governments are just looking for excuses to regulate discourse and enforce censorship these days.  I don't mean to deny the terrible harm that's done to young people via digital media.  I'm passionate about free speech, but I don't know if I'm an absolutist.  I just don't trust the institutions in their current conditions and with their present leaders, and in the case of the European Union, I don't think there's enough of a direct electoral mandate to confer the authority to exercise such power.

It's painful to me that a lot of the work to control speech over the last decade has used left-wing principles as reasons or alibis for censoring or silencing people.  For most of my life, over several decades, a multifarious big-tent Western left has been broadly supportive of free speech, until the past ten or fifteen years.  A vibrant counter-culture, which I'm no longer able to locate, has absolutely depended on it.  The experience of the last decade, during which the establishment Left became comfortable with censorship and regulation of speech "for the right reason", has been so unpleasant that I'm inclined to resist further state efforts to control speech, for the time being.

I am so grateful to editors  like Arthur Gelb, Marvin Siegel, Mike Leahy and  Irv Molotsky and reporters such as Murray Schumach, David Bird, Larry Van Gelder, Al Clark and many more for their guidance and their support. Remembering Tim

My brother Tim became habituated to drink — to the inhibitions lifted from him by his delicious, insidious beer — that giving, forgiving, and tragically taking, party-loving friend.

Tim was good at holding his alcohol, drinking a case or two of brew at a dangerous, daily pace — with grace, while nary (nearly) exhibiting signs of decline, slurring, fumbling, or stumbling. But then his merrymaking friend, who was always the giver, took hold of Tim. And his liver.

Dive bars, smashed cars, and seeing stars were part of the malady of Tim’s drinking revelry as family and friends witnessed his end — the tragedy of him drowning in drink.

Tim lived this aphorism of alcoholism:
The man takes a drink.
The drink takes a drink.
The drink takes the man.

Tim was a kind, loving soul who tried to fill, or rather climb out of — if only for some happy times — a deep, dark hole inside.

I love you and miss you, brother.

Tim Rowley
2 July 1959 – 4 February 2025

The “initiative was originally intended to raise trillions of dollars needed to combat climate change. But with President Trump leading the United States, which is the bank’s largest shareholder, Mr. Banga has been shifting the organization’s ambitions toward infrastructure and job creation.”

Probably the worst impacts from this bill will stem from the rollback on climate change actions.

The climate crisis was already looking as if we'd left it too late, but the election of Trump may be the final straw.

The sudden uptick in global temperatures in March 2023 has been enough to produce even more enhanced extreme weather events, and at some point there'll be harvest failures in multiple regions in several successive years.

The politicians will of course blame migrants.

Certainly each degree point matters, but there are thresholds and we are nudging them.

The probability now is that by 2100 the global average temperature will be at least 3 C deg over pre-industrial. I don't know how we get through that. I've always tried to hold tight to the science, rejecting denialism, rejecting unevidenced doomerism. We can't fool ourselves, this is bad.

comments.name: Pat hayes
comments.body: Last year the Swawilla Basin fire held at the top of the Keller Ridge a half-mile from our school. This year the community was under Level 2 evacuation, Get Ready, for three weeks, sandwiched between Kaiser Canyon and Modrite fires. In both cases our campus was used as fire camp headquarters for 500+ personnel. Population of our community is about 200 and our enrollment is a total of 60. The school, the Clinic, the Community Center, store and Post Office all sit on a scant five acres so a serious wildfire would likely take everything. Hardening the school, adding emergency services infrastructure such as power generation, is on my list as the grant finder and resource coordinator because if we lose the school the community dies.

Had Vitale been approached by Armani while still designing Miu Miu, his hands tied perhaps with a non-compete clause? Was his excepting the Versace position, with the very public secret that Prada was purchasing, a means to get them to fire him, knowing the ref Simons had always/only intended to insert Mulier as head creative at Versace, and thereby dissolve his non-compete so Armani could be a reality sooner than later? Surely Prada HAD TO save face by not firing Vitale before he created a collection. Kudos to Mr. Vitale if he is this clever...That is my guess, if anyone cares. Or do we believe Mr. Vitale was so confident in his ability that he knew he would kill that singular collection (which he did...who is this silly person who didn't understand and called it tacky..it was invigorating) and cause such an uproar in fashion-land that he could sit back and wait for the offers. comments.name: stephan morrow

I went for 9 years to Telluride until the millennium but IMHO all these festivals have gone corporate. As much of a marketplace as Sundance - a far cry from what Redford had in mind & Toronto just behind The New York Film Festival. So this whole universe of festivals as being an alternative to Hollywood product, has been lost. You're competing with multi-million dollar films now with celebrities galore. Gone are the days when 'Get Thee Out' up at Telluride - a Russian  (I think) gem & hung out with the director who had a brother in Brooklyn. Or Raul Ruiz's Time Regained (which I had to see twice). Tom Luddy RIP. Or hanging out w/John Michael Hayes alone to receive a personal lesson in film writing. (I couldn't quite grok how after making 2 Hitchcock films he would end up teaching at a college. Or for that matter, Alexander Mackendrick, the director of significant Sweet Smell of Success.  But the world turns so that it seems that the original impulse for independent films has disappeared & been replaced by a farm team for the big leagues. & now there's even a glitch in the smaller film festival arena: so many are being established that are nothing more than a scam to have filmmakers send in entry fees - or they give out so many awards that almost everybody can go away claiming an award (meaningless). Ultimately you end up in the same conondrum as the old days: how do you become a filmmaker? Raise the budget" And now - that's millions.
Artistic Director
Great Am Play Series

comments.name: NYC Municipal Employee
comments.body:
Integrity is doing the right thing when no one is watching.  There are 250,000 NYC municipal retires and exponentially more of their friends, family member and neighbors watching to see if you truly care about and support, retired NYC first responders, teachers, healthcare workers, sanitization workers and their colleagues. 

Seventeen NYC Council members have gone on record supporting critical legislation, for which countless individuals are grateful.  However, to date, as a collective unit, the City Council has failed to demonstrate respect, compassion and support for those that built the city, and rebuilt it numerous times. Many current Council members were educated by "us", you received care from "us" and support from "us" when you and your loved ones most needed help;

For decades, we worked hard, we followed  the rules, we were promised traditional Medicare coupled with premium free supplemental insurance. Uphold the promise.

THANK YOU to the seventeen city council members who have signed onto support intro 1008-2008.

For the few placing self-interests, political ambitions, personal relationships and ego ahead of 250,000 vulnerable, elderly, infirm and disabled human beings, these choices will likely serve as the basis for your legacy. They will be the foundation of NYC’s reputation as an employer reneging on its promises to its labor force. The same people who claim in photo ops and on social media to never forget and honor those who came before.
